Photograph: Pest Free Purerua New Zealand Nine Lives, the feral cat that terrorised New Zealand’s rare ducks, is caught after three years Large tabby cat that wiped out dozens of rare pāteke, or brown teal, has been killed after eluding trappers with its ‘very erratic’ behaviour Eva Corlett in Wellington Tue 4 Aug 2026 01.45 EDT Last modified on Tue 4 Aug 2026 02.12 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A notorious feral cat given the name “Nine Lives” because it eluded trappers for three years has been caught and killed in New Zealand , ending its devastating rampage against one of the country’s rare duck populations. The cat, a large grey tabby, is estimated to have killed dozens of New Zealand’s rarest mainland duck – or 1% of its population – plus a host of kiwi chicks, native geckos and other native wildlife during the three years it was known to be roaming the Purerua peninsula, near the top of the North Island. “We don’t take for granted that we’ve had this success because it had us baffled for so long,” said Andy Mentor, the project manager for Pest Free Purerua, a conservation project. ‘Coming home’: kiwi enter parliament for first time as New Zealand marks conservation win Read more New Zealand has one of the highest rates of cat ownership in the world, and the impact of feral and domestic cats on biodiversity ignites fierce debate. Some on social media were horrified Nine Lives had been shot, believing it deserved to live, while others said its capture was “a fantastic result”. Nine Lives will form part of that debate long after its death, with its body set to be taxidermied for use as a tool to educate the community about the devastating impact of feral cats on native species. Nine Lives was first spotted on the Purerua peninsula in Northland in 2023. What ensued was a frustrating and twisted game of cat and mouse. View image in fullscreen Nine Lives ate dozens of pāteke, or brown teal, that were being introduced back into the wild. Photograph: Pest Free Purerua Pest Free Purerua had just introduced 20 pāteke, or brown teal – the country’s rarest mainland duck – to the peninsula, believing it had control over the feral cat population. “But within a week we had our first death. We put up some cameras and we identified a particular cat with specific markings,” Mentor said. Another 15 pāteke were killed, with the same cat turning up. “It was a really stressful time. So we brought in more traps, gear, night cameras to try and get to the root cause of the problem.” The project managed to catch other feral cats over the next year, but Nine Lives remained elusive. They decided to release more pāteke in 2024 but the same cat appeared, killing another 15 of the 20 birds. “This particular cat would be very erratic. It would show up in a particular place and then not show up for another two or three months. It would show up in the dusk, midnight, early morning, through the day, so it was never a predictable pattern, which made it very, very difficult to track,” Mentor said. The team came close to catching it on a number of occasions, but each time it slipped their grasp, earning it the name Nine Lives. At the end of July, Mentor and his team noticed the cat had turned up to a quarry three nights in a row, which was “quite unusual”. They laid out salmon, fried chicken and rabbit to attract the animal, and deployed cages and traps. On 30 July, a notification on a cellphone camera showed a cat in one of the cages. “We dispatched our trappers to check it out and there it was. So it was humanely shot,” Mentor said. The animal will have its stomach contents examined to see what it was feeding on before being taxidermied. Mentor said it has likely also fed on kiwi chicks, native geckos and other native wildlife. More than 2.5m feral cats roam New Zealand’s bush and on offshore islands, where they can grow up to a metre long, including their tail. They have destroyed native wildlife and hunted some bird species to the brink of extinction. In November, the government announced feral cats would be added to the country’s world-leading Predator-Free 2050 strategy. Mentor said moving from the suppression of cats to an elimination strategy will be a “real step up” for the peninsula and the team may restart introducing pāteke once more. But for now, conservationists will celebrate the capture of Nine Lives, as well as honour their most evasive adversary. “Nine Lives needs to be given a certain amount of dignity and respect,” said Mentor. Linert Contact Us Contact Advertise Submit News Statement of Values Terms of Service Public Notices Browse notices Place a notice Latest News ’26 report cards show ups, downs Youngstown City Schools make ‘historic’ gain By Brandon Cantwell September 16, 2026 7 min read Trending A new academic year is in full swing, and districts across the Mahoning Valley are learning what leaps -- or steps back -- they took over the past year, as Ohio hands out its report cards. Released Tuesday morning, these assessments offer insight into how schools in the Valley are faring across several key metrics, from early literacy to student progress and graduation rates. The Ohio Department of Education and Workforce evaluates public schools and districts annually based on a series of metrics designed to gauge not only student performance, but also how well schools support growth in areas like literacy, preparation for post-graduation and the academic progress of historically underserved groups. Each component of the ODE's assessment gives a one- to five-star rating for achievement, progress, gap closing, graduation and early literacy: ● 1 to 1 1/2 stars means districts need significant support to meet state standards; ● 2 to 2 1/2 stars means the district needs support to meet state standards; ● 3 to 3 1/2 stars means the district meets state standards; ● 4 to 4 1/2 stars means the district exceeds state standards; ● 5 stars means the district significantly exceeds state standards. The report cards show a five-year high of 62.2% in literacy proficiency following districts completing their first full year with the implementation of Science of Reading, according to a news release from Gov. Mike DeWine's office. The Science of Reading is a statewide initiative launched in 2023 as part of the state's operating budget to overhaul literacy instruction by mandating phonics-based literacy instruction and outlawing three-cueing, a method that encourages students to guess words with context clues. In Mahoning County, it was business as usual for many districts, with Boardman, Austintown, Canfield and Poland receiving the same ratings as last year. Several districts showed improvement, with Youngstown, Lowellville and Sebring receiving a slight bump. YOUNGSTOWN Youngstown City School District Superintendent Jeremy Batchelor said two district schools -- Youngstown Rayen Early College and Choffin Career & Technical Center -- received five-star ratings, while Rayen Early College Middle School received four stars. Youngstown received a three-star rating overall, which was a half-star increase from 2025. "With Youngstown City School District officially earning a three-star overall rating on the latest Ohio State Report Card, we are overwhelmed with pride," Batchelor said. "This achievement shows our district meets state standards, a historic milestone for YCSD since the introduction of state report cards. We are also honored to celebrate a four-year 90.7% graduation rate, marking another significant accomplishment for our district since Ohio began measuring graduation rates." Batchelor said the progress is the result of dedication by district teachers, staff and administration, "combined with our scholars' hard work and the unwavering support of our families. While we have made great strides, we remain committed to continuous improvement." "YCSD remains dedicated to building an even brighter future for every scholar in Youngstown." AUSTINTOWN The Austintown Local School District retained its four-star rating from last year. "Our four-star overall rating reflects the strong work taking place across Austintown Local Schools. Earning five stars in both Gap Closing and Graduation Rate is a significant accomplishment and shows the impact of our staff's commitment to students," said Superintendent Timothy Kelty. "The statistics give us a clear direction, and we are already taking targeted steps to continue to strengthen instruction, accelerate student growth, and improve outcomes across every building. We are incredibly proud of the dedication of our staff and the hard work of our students. " BOARDMAN Boardman also retained its ranking from last year at three-and-half stars. The district was able to maintain its 3.5-star rating, while increasing its College, Career, Workforce, and Military Readiness component by two stars, according to Superintendent Chris Neifer. "We feel that gain is a byproduct of the district placing an emphasis on project based learning, and our push for STEAM education and life skills courses. Boardman is very proud of our Advanced Placement and College Credit Plus participation and achievements at the high school level. While this is not directly reflected in the State Report Card, it is a component of the CCWMR." "While analyzing the data, we realize we missed the four-star rating by the slimmest of margins, and the district will continue its focus on student improvement and success. Year after year, Boardman Schools remain steadfast in our pursuit of real-world opportunities at all grade levels that will prepare our students for the rapidly changing world we face," Neifer added. CANFIELD The Canfield Local School District received a four-and-a-half star rating, maintaining its ranking from 2025. However, the district received five stars in achievement, gap closing and graduation, four stars in progress and after graduation readiness, and three stars in early literacy. "I am extremely proud of the work our kids and staff do every day," said Canfield Board of Education President Steve Demaiolo. Both C.H. Campbell Elementary School and Canfield Village Middle School received five stars, while Hilltop Elementary and the high school received 4.5 stars. "Most of our strongest scores held steady: Achievement, Gap Closing and Graduation are still fives, Overall Progress is still a four. Readiness for college and career jumped from a two to a four -- that's our biggest gain. Early Literacy dipped one level, from a four to a three -- that's the one area we want to be upfront about," Superintendent Joe Knoll said. "Two areas for improvement: our youngest readers' growth softened this year (Early Literacy dropped from a four to a three), and we also saw softer reading growth in the middle school. Those two things are connected -- we've seen a pattern where reading growth tends to slow down as kids move from elementary into middle school, and this year it showed up more clearly than usual," Knoll added. "We're already acting on it. Elementary teachers have been analyzing the data building by building, we've rolled out a stronger, research-based approach to teaching reading (Science of Reading), and we're paying closer attention to that elementary-to-middle-school transition specifically, rather than waiting for it to show up again next year." POLAND The Poland Local School District earned a four-star rating, which is the same as last year. "We are very pleased that Poland Local Schools earned an overall four-star rating, which reflects performance that exceeds Ohio's state standards," said Poland Superin-tendent Andrew J. Tommelleo. "We are especially proud of receiving five-star ratings in both Gap Closing and Graduation, as those measures speak directly to our commitment to ensuring all students are supported and that students leave Poland prepared for their future." Tommelleo said these results reflect the outstanding efforts of students, teachers, staff, families and the community. He said Poland Local Schools has a strong tradition of high expectations, excellent instruction and meaningful support systems for students. As for the categories that need improvement, Tommelleo said, "While we are proud of the district's overall performance, we remain committed to helping every student achieve a year's worth of growth and beyond. Continuous improvement has always been part of our culture, and we are confident that the work already underway will positively impact student growth." SEBRING Sebring schools improved a half-star from last year to earn a four-star rating this year. "In Sebring we are very pleased with the progress and growth in our building. The collective efforts of our entire learning community are evidenced in our rating moving from 2.5 stars two years ago to four-star "Exceeding Expectations" rating. It is our highest rating ever," said Brian Clark, principal of Sebring Junior/Senior High School. "We are proud to tout the 100% graduation rating the past several school years, which was a feat not accomplished in well over two decades in Sebring. Preparing every student for their future in the Valley's workforce is further evidenced in Ohio's newest rating area of College, Career, Workforce and Military Readiness, where we are among Ohio's very best five-star schools." Photograph: kali9/Getty Images Pennsylvania Nine people, including children, dead after mass shooting in Pennsylvania Authorities say suspect among dead in house after standoff with police in Erie and there is no ongoing threat Marina Dunbar Sat 10 Oct 2026 11.45 EDT Last modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 11.47 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Nine people, including children, died in a mass murder on Friday in Erie, Pennsylvania , after a gun-wielding attacker opened fire outside a home and then entered the property, according to authorities. The suspected attacker was also found dead as police responded to the deadly violence, which triggered a standoff involving Erie police officers and tactical teams. Police discovered the killings at about 5pm when officers were called to a residence following reports of gunfire. Witnesses told authorities that they had seen an attacker with a gun outside the property before making his way inside. US man arrested as second suspect in Canada mass school shooting planned with ChatGPT Read more Responding officers discovered two women lying dead in the street, both having suffered fatal gunshot wounds. The situation quickly developed into a standoff as police officers and tactical personnel surrounded the residence. More gunshots were heard coming from inside the home, and officers entered the place. Inside, police said they made a devastating discovery, finding seven additional victims, including children, along with the suspected attacker. Investigators believe the attacker died from a self-inflicted gunshot wound. Erie’s police chief, Rick Lorah, spoke about the scale of the mass murder, describing the scene as among the most distressing and heartbreaking he had witnessed. “The loss of life is devastating and the circumstances we are working through are deeply disturbing,” Lorah said. “At this time, we can confirm that the suspect is deceased. Based on the information currently available to us, there is no ongoing threat to the public.” He added: “Our hearts are with the victims, their families and everyone affected by this tragedy. There are no words that can adequately express the magnitude of the loss of life here.” Authorities on Saturday said they were still investigating the circumstances surrounding the killings, with authorities attempting to determine a motive for the violence. The city of Erie also issued a statement on social media confirming that the suspected shooter had died and that the immediate danger had passed. The statement described the case as a “terrible tragedy”, although the city’s statement did not provide further information about the events leading up to the shooting. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Around 2-3 times a day Sign up to Breaking News US Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion “We understand that the news brings deep shock and sorrow to our residents, and we want to assure the public that the situation has been contained,” the city said. Figures from the Gun Violence Archive indicate that the killings in Erie marked at least the 19th mass murder of the year. Such cases are defined as ones in which four or more victims are murdered. Many of those mass murders have been what are considered family annihilations , in which an attacker kills multiple close family members. The nonpartisan archive also indicated that the killings in Erie were among more than 500 mass shootings across the US since the beginning of January. Mass shootings are defined as cases in which four or more victims are shot whether fatally or non-fatally. Mass shootings for years have remained a persistent problem in the US, often intensifying public demands for stronger gun control measures at the federal level. Despite those calls, Congress has not enacted such restrictions sought over the years.
